info.title: FixFlow Manufacturer API
info.description:
The **FixFlow Manufacturer API** is the machine surface of a manufacturer's own systems
(warranty desk, CRM, reporting). It is authenticated by an API key, versioned in the path, and
documented by this single artefact: the document you are reading **is** the contract.

This is release **1.0.0**, the first released version of `v1`. The endpoints listed below are its
whole surface; later releases only add to it and record every change in the
[Changelog](#changelog).

## Base URL

Every path in this document is relative to the API base of your FixFlow deployment:

```
https://<your-fixflow-host>/fixflow
```

So the verify-key call below is `GET https://<your-fixflow-host>/fixflow/manufacturer-api/v1/key`.
Your FixFlow contact gives you the host; the `/fixflow` segment is part of the base and does not
change.

## Getting a key

Use one key per integrating system, never one per person. There are two ways to get one:

- **Self-service**: sign in to the FixFlow manufacturer portal and open **API keys**. Any active
  user of your company can create and revoke your company's keys there.
- **Through FixFlow staff**: ask your FixFlow contact, naming the system that will use the key
  (for example `Warranty desk`).

Either way:

1. The full key value is shown **once**, at creation time, and is never retrievable again. Store it
   in your secret manager immediately.
2. Call `GET /manufacturer-api/v1/key` to confirm the key works and to see which manufacturer it is
   bound to.

A key can be revoked at any time; a revoked key is rejected from the next request on. To rotate,
create a new key, deploy it, then revoke the old one. Several keys can be active at once, so
rotation needs no downtime.

## Authentication

Send the key in the `X-Api-Key` request header on **every** call:

```http
GET /fixflow/manufacturer-api/v1/key HTTP/1.1
Host: <your-fixflow-host>
X-Api-Key: ffmfr_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
```

Rules that will not change within `v1`:

- `X-Api-Key` is the only accepted credential. A bearer token (JWT) from the FixFlow web portals is
  **not** accepted here, and a Manufacturer API key is **not** accepted outside
  `/manufacturer-api/v1/*`.
- The manufacturer is taken from the key alone. There is no `manufacturerId` parameter to pass, and
  no way to read another manufacturer's data with your key — rows that are not yours do not exist
  for the API.
- Always use HTTPS. A key sent over plain HTTP must be treated as leaked and revoked.

## Demo client

A small MIT-licensed reference client (Node.js, TypeScript) shows the whole integration end to end:

- verifying the key;
- creating work orders with safe retries;
- the polling loop over the change feed with a stored cursor;
- handling `429`.

It runs against a built-in mock of this API, so you can try it before you have a key. Once you
give it your base URL and a key, it works against your FixFlow deployment. The key stays on the
client's server and never reaches a browser.

**Repository:** coming soon. The public link will be published here.

## Creating a work order

`POST /manufacturer-api/v1/work-orders` submits a repair request for one of your units at an end
customer's site. You do not need to know any FixFlow identifier: send the customer, the service
address and the unit, and FixFlow matches them against its own directories or creates the missing
rows. The work order opens in status `New` and a dispatcher takes it from there; you do not choose
the service company.

The response is the **work-order resource** — the same shape every read returns.

### Idempotency

`externalReference` is your own claim or case number and is **required**. It is the idempotency key,
unique per manufacturer:

- the first call with a given value creates the work order and answers `201 Created` with a
  `Location` header;
- every later call with the same value answers `200 OK` with that **same, unchanged** work order and
  the response header `Idempotent-Replayed: true`;
- two calls that race each other still produce exactly one work order.

So retrying a request that timed out is always safe, and you never need a "did it get through?"
lookup before retrying. The replay never changes anything: send corrected data under a **new**
`externalReference`, or ask the dispatcher.

### How the customer is matched

The customer of the work order is the **end customer** whose unit is broken — not you.

1. If you send `customer.reference` (the customer's id in your system) and we have already seen it,
   that customer is used — even if the name or address in this request differs. The stored customer
   is never overwritten from a request.
2. Otherwise we look for a customer with the same name **and** a site at the same
   `addressLine1` + ZIP. Name alone is never enough: two unrelated companies may share a name.
3. Otherwise a new customer is created.

In cases 2 and 3 a `customer.reference` you sent is remembered and points at that customer from then
on. Sending `customer.reference` consistently is the only way to guarantee one customer record.

### How the service location is matched

Among that customer's sites we look for the same `addressLine1` + ZIP, otherwise we create the site
(named `serviceLocation.name`, or the street line if you omit it). ZIP matching uses the first five
digits, so `08608` and `08608-1234` are the same place. Comparisons ignore letter case and extra
spaces.

### How the unit is matched

The unit always belongs to the manufacturer your key is bound to. Matching only ever looks at your
own units at that site — equipment of another brand is never matched and never modified, even if it
carries the same serial number or model.

- With `equipment.serialNumber` we match on the serial number.
- Without it we match on `equipment.modelNumber`, but only if there is exactly one such unit at the
  site. Several identical models, or none, means there is nothing to match safely.
- Otherwise a new unit is created under your brand.

`equipment.modelNumber` is required. If it is in your model catalogue in FixFlow the unit is linked
to that model; an unknown model number is kept as free text, so nothing is rejected over it.

### Validation

A body that fails validation answers `422` with `errors` keyed by the JSON path of the field, for
example `customer.name` or `serviceLocation.zip`. All problems are reported at once. Unknown fields
in the body are ignored.

## Tracking status

There are no webhooks in `v1`. You poll, and we make polling cheap: the **change feed** tells you
which of your work orders moved, so you never re-read the ones that did not.

The three reads all return the same work-order resource, and all of them see the same scope — every
work order whose unit is one of your brand's, not only the ones you created through this API,
**including archived ones** (they come back with `archivedAt` set, so archiving reads as a state and
not as a disappearance):

| Call | Use it for |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /manufacturer-api/v1/work-orders/changes` | The normal loop: what changed since last time |
| `GET /manufacturer-api/v1/work-orders?ids=…&references=…` | Resync: re-read up to 100 at once |
| `GET /manufacturer-api/v1/work-orders/{id}` and `/by-reference/{externalReference}` | One work order, on demand |

### The polling loop

1. **Subscribe.** Call `changes` once with no parameters. You get `items: []` and a `nextCursor`
   that means "from now on". Store that cursor where it survives a restart.
2. **Poll.** Every **30–60 seconds** call `changes?cursor=<stored cursor>`. Apply the `items`, then
   store the new `nextCursor` — ideally in the same transaction, so a crash cannot lose it.
3. **Drain.** While the answer says `hasMore: true`, more changes are already waiting: call again
   right away with the cursor you just stored instead of waiting for the next tick.
4. **Resync** if you ever lose the cursor or suspect your copy is stale: read the work orders you
   care about with the batch call, then subscribe again.

```http
GET /fixflow/manufacturer-api/v1/work-orders/changes?cursor=djE6ODgxNDI&limit=100 HTTP/1.1
X-Api-Key: ffmfr_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
```

```json
{
  "items": [
    { "id": 10427, "status": "Done", "changedAt": "2026-10-13T15:48:02Z" }
  ],
  "nextCursor": "djE6ODgxNTA",
  "hasMore": false
}
```

(`items` entries are full work-order resources; the one above is abridged.)

### Rules of the feed

- **Items are snapshots, not events.** Each item is the work order exactly as it is now, plus
  `changedAt` — when we last saw it change. Several changes to one work order inside one page
  collapse into a single item, and the feed never tells you which field moved.
- **Delivery is at-least-once, so be idempotent.** The same snapshot can arrive twice — after a
  retry, or simply because you reused a cursor. Apply items by `id` (upsert), never by counting
  them.
- **The cursor is opaque.** Store the string verbatim; do not parse it, order it or build one
  yourself. An invalid cursor answers `422`, and the fix is a resync, not a retry.
- **A moved cursor with an empty page is normal.** Changes to work orders outside your scope move
  the cursor without being shown.
- **The feed lags a few seconds behind live** by design, so that a change committed slightly out of
  order is never skipped. Status changes therefore reach you a few seconds after they happen.
- `limit` is 1–500, 100 by default. `since=<ISO-8601 instant>` starts from a moment instead of
  subscribing from now; `cursor` wins when you send both.

Changes to any of these resource fields put a work order on the feed: `status` (and with it the
stage timestamps and `completedAt`), `urgency`, `description`, `deadline`, `isWarranty`,
`warrantyNumber`, `scheduledServiceAt`, the unit, and `archivedAt`.

A work order that leaves your scope — a dispatcher relinks the unit to another brand — stops being
readable (`404` / `notFound`) and does **not** produce a feed item.

### Reading a batch

`ids` and `references` take comma-separated lists and may be mixed, up to **100 identifiers in
total**; more answers `422`. Unknown identifiers, another manufacturer's, and work orders no longer
in your scope all come back under `notFound`, echoed exactly as you sent them — one bad identifier
never fails the whole call.

```json
{
  "items": [],
  "notFound": { "ids": [99999], "references": ["CLM-UNKNOWN"] }
}
```

## Errors

Every error response is a [`ProblemDetails`](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457) body with the
content type `application/problem+json`:

```json
{
  "title": "Unauthorized",
  "detail": "A valid API key is required.",
  "status": 401
}
```

| Status | When | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `401 Unauthorized` | The `X-Api-Key` header is missing, empty, unknown or revoked — or a JWT was sent instead of a key. | Fix the credential. Do not retry with the same key. |
| `404 Not Found` | The addressed resource does not exist **or** belongs to another manufacturer — the two cases are deliberately indistinguishable. | Check the identifier; do not treat it as "exists but forbidden". |
| `422 Unprocessable Entity` | The request body or query failed validation. `errors` carries the per-field messages. | Fix the payload; retrying unchanged will fail again. |
| `429 Too Many Requests` | The per-key rate limit is exhausted. | Wait `Retry-After` seconds, then retry. |
| `400 Bad Request` | The request could not be parsed or bound at all (malformed JSON, wrong parameter type). | Fix the request. |
| `409 Conflict` | A write collided with the current state of the data. | Re-read the resource and decide. |

`5xx` responses are our fault. They are safe to retry with backoff for idempotent requests
(`GET`); report them if they persist.

## Rate limits

Requests are counted **per key** in a one-minute sliding window; the default allowance is **120
requests per minute**. Over the limit the API answers `429` with a `Retry-After` header in seconds
and no side effects. The limit protects the shared service, so poll on a schedule rather than in a
tight loop, and keep one key per system so one noisy job cannot starve another.

## Versioning policy

The major version lives in the path (`/manufacturer-api/v1/...`) and `info.version` carries the
published document version.

Within `v1` we only make **additive** changes, and your client must tolerate them:

- new endpoints, new optional request fields, new response fields;
- new values in an existing enumeration;
- new `4xx` reasons for input we already rejected.

A **breaking** change — removing or renaming a path, operation, parameter or response field,
narrowing a type, dropping an enumeration value, or making an existing input required — is never
shipped inside `v1`. It goes to `/manufacturer-api/v2`, which is announced before it is released and
runs alongside `v1`.

This is enforced on our side, not promised in prose: release `1.0.0` of this document is frozen as a
compatibility baseline, and our build compares every later document against it. A change that
removes or narrows anything, or makes an input required, fails the build before it can be released.

Practical client rules: ignore unknown response fields, treat unknown enumeration values as
"unmapped" instead of failing, and never depend on property order or on the exact wording of
`title`/`detail`.

## Changelog

### 1.0.0 — 2026-10-10 — initial release

The first released version of the contract, and the compatibility baseline of `v1`:

- `GET /manufacturer-api/v1/key` — verify a key and read the manufacturer it is bound to.
- `POST /manufacturer-api/v1/work-orders` — create a work order; idempotent on `externalReference`
  (`200` + `Idempotent-Replayed: true` on a repeat).
- `GET /manufacturer-api/v1/work-orders/{id}` and
  `GET /manufacturer-api/v1/work-orders/by-reference/{externalReference}` — read one work order;
  unknown, another manufacturer's and out-of-scope all answer `404`.
- `GET /manufacturer-api/v1/work-orders?ids=…&references=…` — read up to 100 at once →
  `{ items, notFound }`.
- `GET /manufacturer-api/v1/work-orders/changes` — the change feed with an opaque cursor →
  `{ items, nextCursor, hasMore }`; see [Tracking status](#tracking-status).
- Reads see archived work orders too (`archivedAt` is set on them).
- `X-Api-Key` authentication, `ProblemDetails` errors, per-key rate limit.

The `1.0.0-preview`, `1.1.0-preview` and `1.2.0-preview` documents published while the API was being
built are superseded by this release. Nothing that was in them was removed or narrowed.

post.description:
Submits a repair request for one of your units at an end customer's site. FixFlow matches or creates the customer, the service location and the unit itself, then opens the work order in status `New` for a dispatcher to triage.

`externalReference` — your own claim or case number — is the idempotency key: the first call creates the work order (`201`), every later call with the same value returns that same work order unchanged (`200` with the `Idempotent-Replayed: true` header). Retrying a timed-out request is therefore always safe.

The unit always belongs to the manufacturer the key is bound to, so the work order shows up in your scope by construction; equipment of another brand is never matched or modified.

x-codeSamples.label: curl
x-codeSamples.source:
# work-order.json holds the request body shown above.
curl -X POST "https://<your-fixflow-host>/fixflow/manufacturer-api/v1/work-orders" \
  -H "X-Api-Key: $FIXFLOW_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data @work-order.json

# A retry with the same externalReference is safe: it returns
# the same work order (200, header Idempotent-Replayed: true).

get.summary: Read a batch of work orders
get.description:
Reads up to 100 work orders in one call, addressed by FixFlow ids (`ids`), by your own references (`references`), or by both. Each parameter takes a comma-separated list and may also be repeated.

`items` carries the work orders that are yours, ordered by id. Everything else — unknown, another manufacturer's, or no longer in your scope — is echoed back under `notFound`, exactly as you asked for it, so one unknown identifier never fails the whole call.

This is the resync tool: when the change feed's cursor is lost or your copy looks stale, re-read the work orders you care about in batches of 100.

parameters.name: ids
parameters.description: FixFlow work-order ids, comma-separated (the parameter may also be repeated).

parameters.name: references
parameters.description: Your own `externalReference` values, comma-separated (the parameter may also be repeated).

items.description: Unit shuts down after 10 minutes and reports error E-14.

ids: At most 100 identifiers (ids and references combined) can be read at once.

x-codeSamples.label: curl
x-codeSamples.source:
# Up to 100 ids and references in total.
curl "https://<your-fixflow-host>/fixflow/manufacturer-api/v1/work-orders?ids=10427,10431&references=CLM-2026-55120" \
  -H "X-Api-Key: $FIXFLOW_API_KEY"

get.description:
Returns the current state of one of your work orders by its FixFlow id.

The scope is every work order whose unit is one of your brand's — not only the ones you created through this API — and it includes **archived** work orders, which come back with `archivedAt` set so an archived request reads as a state rather than as a disappearance.

A work order that does not exist, is not yours, or carries no catalogued unit all answer the same `404`: the API never confirms that a row exists.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: The FixFlow work-order id, as returned in `id`.

example.description: Unit shuts down after 10 minutes and reports error E-14.

get.summary: Read one work order by your own reference
get.description:
Same as reading by id, but addressed with the `externalReference` you sent when you created the work order — so you never have to store FixFlow ids.

References are scoped to your key: another manufacturer's reference, a reference you never used, and a work order that has since left your scope all answer `404`.

parameters.name: externalReference
parameters.description: The `externalReference` you sent when creating the work order.

example.description: Unit shuts down after 10 minutes and reports error E-14.

get.description:
Streams the work orders of yours that changed, so you never have to re-read the ones that did not. There are no webhooks in `v1`: this feed is how you track state.

**The loop.** Call it once without parameters — you get no items and a `nextCursor` that means "from now on". Persist that cursor, then every 30–60 seconds call again with it; each answer gives you the changed work orders plus a new cursor to persist. While `hasMore` is `true` there are already more changes waiting, so you may keep calling immediately instead of waiting for the next tick.

**Items are snapshots, not diffs.** Each item is the work order exactly as it is now, plus `changedAt` — when we last saw it change. Several changes to one work order inside one page collapse into one item.

**Be idempotent.** Delivery is at-least-once: the same snapshot can arrive twice, so apply items by id rather than counting events. For the same reason the feed deliberately lags a few seconds behind live, and a page can come back empty with a moved cursor (changes to work orders outside your scope advance it without being shown).

`cursor` is opaque — store it verbatim and make no assumptions about its contents. To backfill instead of subscribing, pass `since` with an ISO-8601 instant; `cursor` wins when you send both. If a cursor is ever lost, resync with the batch read.

parameters.name: cursor
parameters.description: The `nextCursor` of your previous page, verbatim. Omit it to subscribe from now on.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: How many changed work orders one page may carry: 1–500, 100 by default.

parameters.name: since
parameters.description: Backfill from this ISO-8601 instant instead of subscribing from now (for example `2026-10-13T15:48:02Z`). Ignored when `cursor` is sent.

items.description: Unit shuts down after 10 minutes and reports error E-14.

cursor: The cursor is not valid. Resync with a batch read, then subscribe again.

x-codeSamples.label: curl
x-codeSamples.source:
# 1. Subscribe from now: no items, just the current nextCursor. Store it.
curl "https://<your-fixflow-host>/fixflow/manufacturer-api/v1/work-orders/changes" \
  -H "X-Api-Key: $FIXFLOW_API_KEY"

# 2. Every 30-60 s: pass the last nextCursor verbatim and store the new one.
#    While hasMore is true, call again straight away.
curl "https://<your-fixflow-host>/fixflow/manufacturer-api/v1/work-orders/changes?cursor=$CURSOR&limit=100" \
  -H "X-Api-Key: $FIXFLOW_API_KEY"

# Backfill from a moment in time instead of a cursor:
curl "https://<your-fixflow-host>/fixflow/manufacturer-api/v1/work-orders/changes?since=2026-10-01T00:00:00Z" \
  -H "X-Api-Key: $FIXFLOW_API_KEY"

ApiKey.description: Manufacturer API key, created on the API keys page of the manufacturer portal or by FixFlow staff, and shown once at creation time. The manufacturer is taken from the key; a portal bearer token is not accepted here.
ApiKey.name: X-Api-Key
